facts.claim: The 2021 statement made no changes to the 2007 AHA recommendations; prophylaxis is still limited to the 4 categories at highest risk of a bad outcome from viridans streptococcal IE.

cites.quote: These guidelines were updated by a 2021 scientific statement by the AHA that recommended no changes to the 2007 guideline recommendations.

facts.claim: Conditions for which prophylaxis is suggested: (a) prosthetic cardiac valve or prosthetic material: a prosthetic valve, transcatheter-implanted prosthetic valves, valve repair with devices (annuloplasty rings, clips), and LVADs or implantable hearts; (b) previous, relapsed or recurrent IE; (c) congenital heart disease: unrepaired cyanotic CHD (including palliative shunts and conduits); a CHD defect completely repaired with prosthetic material or a device (surgical or transcatheter) during the first 6 months after the procedure; repaired CHD with residual defects at or next to a prosthetic patch or device; surgical or transcatheter pulmonary artery valve or conduit (e.g., Melody valve, Contegra conduit); (d) cardiac transplant recipients who develop valvulopathy.

cites.quote: prosthetic cardiac valves, including transcatheter-implanted prostheses and homografts; prosthetic material used for cardiac valve repair, such as annuloplasty rings and chords; a history of infective endocarditis
with valve regurgitation due to a structurally abnormal valve
completely repaired with prosthetic material or a device for the first six months after the repair procedure

facts.claim: Prophylaxis is not suggested for: pacemakers and similar implantable electronic devices, septal closure devices once closure is complete, peripheral vascular grafts and patches (including hemodialysis grafts), coronary or other vascular stents, CNS ventriculoatrial shunts, vena cava filters, pledgets. Rheumatic heart disease, bicuspid aortic valve, mitral valve prolapse and other native valve disease were reviewed and not added.

cites.quote: Except for the conditions listed above, antibiotic prophylaxis is no longer recommended for any other form of congenital heart disease.

cites.loc: Table 3 and 'Feasibility of including additional high-risk groups', p. e971

facts.claim: Procedures: for the high-risk patients, prophylaxis is suggested for all dental procedures that manipulate gingival tissue or the periapical region of teeth, or perforate the oral mucosa. Not suggested: anesthetic injections through noninfected tissue, radiographs, placing removable prosthodontic or orthodontic appliances, adjusting orthodontic appliances, placing orthodontic brackets, shedding of primary teeth, bleeding from trauma to the lips or mucosa.

cites.quote: prophylaxis is recommended for all dental procedures that involve manipulation of gingival tissue or the periapical region of teeth or perforation of the oral mucosa

facts.claim: Regimen: a single dose 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure. Oral: amoxicillin 2 g (child 50 mg/kg). Cannot take oral: ampicillin 2 g IM or IV (child 50 mg/kg), or cefazolin or ceftriaxone 1 g IM or IV (child 50 mg/kg). Penicillin or ampicillin allergy, oral: cephalexin 2 g (child 50 mg/kg) or another first- or second-generation oral cephalosporin in an equivalent dose; azithromycin or clarithromycin 500 mg (child 15 mg/kg); or doxycycline 100 mg (child under 45 kg: 2.2 mg/kg; 45 kg or more: 100 mg). Allergy and cannot take oral: cefazolin or ceftriaxone 1 g IM or IV (child 50 mg/kg).
facts.conditions: The doses in the table (2 g / 50 mg/kg, etc.) rest on AHA Table 5, which the quote checker cannot open (ahajournals blocks automated access); the ADA quotes confirm only the drug choices.

cites.quote: cephalexin (or other first- or second-generation cephalosporins), azithromycin, clarithromycin, or doxycycline be used as alternatives
the AHA recommends cefazolin or ceftriaxone as alternatives

facts.claim: Clindamycin is no longer recommended (oral or parenteral) for dental prophylaxis: it causes more frequent and severe reactions, including fatal C. difficile infection after a single dose; up to 15% of community-acquired C. difficile may trace to antibiotics prescribed for dental procedures.

cites.quote: no longer recommends use of clindamycin as an oral or parenteral alternative to amoxicillin or ampicillin in individuals with allergies to these drugs

cites.loc: p. e972; Table 5 footnote, p. e973

facts.claim: Do not use a cephalosporin in someone whose penicillin/ampicillin reaction was anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria.

cites.quote: cephalosporins should not be used in an individual with a history of anaphylaxis, angioedema, or urticaria with penicillin or ampicillin

facts.claim: Azithromycin/clarithromycin: caution with a known prolonged QTc (over 450 ms on ECG), torsades risk; doxycycline is the alternative when a penicillin, cephalosporin and macrolide can't be used. About 90% of people labeled penicillin-allergic have negative skin tests; skin testing is suggested if feasible.
facts.conditions: Rests on the AHA statement only (not quote-checked: source blocked to scripts). Don't key an item on the QTc number or the 90% figure until the quote is added.

facts.claim: Forgot the dose: it may be given up to 2 hours after the procedure.

cites.quote: the dosage may be administered up to 2 hours after the procedure

facts.claim: Patient already on a short (7-10 day) antibiotic course: pick an antibiotic from a different class; if possible, delay elective care until 10 days after the course ends. Serial appointments: if possible, wait 10 days after the last dose before the next procedure. Patient on parenteral therapy for IE or another infection: the same parenteral antibiotic may cover the procedure. ADA example: on amoxicillin, use azithromycin or clarithromycin.
facts.conditions: The 10-day waiting periods rest on the AHA statement only (not quote-checked).

cites.quote: recommend that the dentist select an antibiotic from a different class than the one the patient is already taking

facts.claim: Rationale: viridans strep IE is far more likely from daily activities (chewing, toothbrushing, flossing) than from dental procedures; prophylaxis may prevent an exceedingly small number of cases. Good oral health and regular dental care are emphasized.

cites.quote: regularly exposed to oral bacteria during basic daily activities such as brushing or flossing

facts.claim: Scope: adolescents (12+), adults and older adults; after tooth extraction(s) and for temporary management of toothache before definitive care. Key message: nonopioid analgesics, especially an NSAID alone or with acetaminophen, are first-line; opioids are reserved for when first-line therapy is insufficient or contraindicated.

cites.loc: Discussion, Implications for practice and policy
cites.quote: nonopioid medications, particularly NSAIDs alone or in combination with acetaminophen, are first-line therapy for the management of acute dental pain after tooth extraction(s) and toothache in adolescents, adults, and older adults

facts.claim: Suggested starting doses: ibuprofen 400 mg or naproxen sodium 440 mg, alone or with acetaminophen 500 mg. NSAID contraindicated: acetaminophen alone at full dose (e.g., 1,000 mg).

cites.quote: the panel suggests initiating the pain management using an NSAID alone (eg, 400 mg of ibuprofen or 440 mg of naproxen sodium) or in combination with acetaminophen (eg, 500 mg)

facts.claim: Opioids: for simple extractions the panel recommends against opioids (rec. 2). For surgical extractions or toothache, only in rare cases where NSAID ± acetaminophen fails: add or switch to acetaminophen 325 mg + an acetaminophen/opioid combination (e.g., hydrocodone 5-7.5 mg or oxycodone 5 mg) at the lowest dose, fewest tablets and shortest duration, which rarely exceeds 3 days. Avoid "just-in-case" delayed opioid prescriptions.

cites.quote: recommends against the use of opioid analgesics (conditional, low certainty)
325 mg of acetaminophen plus a combination of 325 mg of acetaminophen with an opioid
the shortest duration, which rarely exceeds 3 days
Clinicians should avoid the routine use of just-in-case prescribing of opioids

facts.claim: Maximum daily doses in the guideline: ibuprofen 2,400 mg, naproxen sodium 1,100 mg, acetaminophen 4,000 mg. Warn that acetaminophen-opioid combinations also contain acetaminophen (cumulative dose). Note: the prescription ibuprofen label allows up to 3,200 mg/day for arthritis; key 2,400 mg for dental pain.

cites.quote: The maximum daily dose of ibuprofen is 2,400 mg, naproxen sodium is 1,100 mg, and acetaminophen is 4,000 mg.
Suggested Dosage: 1,200 mg - 3,200 mg daily

facts.claim: Corticosteroids added to standard analgesia after surgical extraction: suggested against. Long-acting LA after extraction: bupivacaine 0.5% with epi 1:200,000 (block or infiltration) or articaine 4% infiltration before discharge (rec. 3). Toothache: short-acting LA (lidocaine 2% or articaine 4% with 1:100,000) for immediate relief (toothache rec. 1).

cites.quote: 0.5% bupivacaine plus 1:200,000 epinephrine by block or infiltration injection

facts.claim: Opioid safety: shared decision making and informed consent covering dependence, misuse, respiratory depression and driving, especially in adolescents and young adults; FDA (2020): discuss naloxone with everyone prescribed an opioid; FDA (2018): tramadol contraindicated under 18 after tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy; codeine and tramadol not recommended in adolescents 12-18 who are obese or have obstructive sleep apnea or severe lung disease; breastfeeding not recommended on codeine or tramadol. In 2019, 39.5% of dentists' opioid prescriptions were "high risk" (e.g., opioid-naive patients given more than a 3-day supply).

cites.quote: In 2019, 39.5% of all opioid prescriptions written by dentists were classified as high risk
A new Contraindication to the tramadol label warning against its use in children younger than 18 years to treat pain after surgery to remove the tonsils and/or adenoids.

facts.claim: NSAID cautions: boxed warning for cardiovascular thrombotic events (MI, stroke) and GI bleeding; contraindicated around CABG surgery; ibuprofen can blunt low-dose aspirin's antiplatelet effect; pregnancy limits in PG-6.

facts.claim: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis (with or without symptomatic apical periodontitis): no antibiotics, whether or not definitive care is immediately available (strong recommendation against when not available; conditional against as an adjunct to definitive care).

cites.quote: The expert panel suggests dentists do not prescribe oral systemic antibiotics as an adjunct to definitive, conservative dental treatment for immunocompetent adults with symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
with or without symptomatic apical periodontitis ‡ (Strong recommendation, low certainty in the evidence)

facts.claim: Pulp necrosis with symptomatic apical periodontitis: no antibiotics (conditional) when definitive care is not immediately available; refer for definitive conservative treatment.

cites.quote: The expert panel suggests dentists do not prescribe oral systemic antibiotics for immunocompetent * adults with pulp necrosis and symptomatic apical periodontitis

facts.claim: Pulp necrosis with localized acute apical abscess (no fascial space spread, fever or malaise): if definitive care is not immediately available, give amoxicillin 500 mg three times a day, 3-7 days, or penicillin VK 500 mg four times a day, 3-7 days (conditional, possibly delayed prescription). As an adjunct when definitive care (pulpectomy, RCT, incision and drainage) is done: no antibiotics (strong).

cites.quote: prescribe oral amoxicillin (500 milligrams, three times a day, 3–7d) or oral penicillin VK (500 milligrams, four times a day, 3–7d) for immunocompetent adults with pulp necrosis and localized acute apical abscess

facts.claim: Acute apical abscess with systemic involvement (fever, malaise, lymph node or fascial space involvement): urgent definitive conservative treatment plus amoxicillin or penicillin VK as in AB-3. Rapidly spreading swelling or airway risk goes to urgent care / ED.

cites.quote: perform urgent definitive, conservative dental treatment in conjunction with prescribing oral amoxicillin (500 milligrams, three times a day, 3–7d) or oral penicillin VK (500 milligrams, four times a day, 3–7d) for immunocompetent adults with pulp necrosis and acute apical abscess with systemic

facts.claim: Amoxicillin is preferred over penicillin VK (better against gram-negative anaerobes, fewer GI effects). Penicillin allergy without anaphylaxis, angioedema or hives: cephalexin 500 mg four times a day, 3-7 days. With anaphylaxis/angioedema/hives history: azithromycin 500 mg day 1, then 250 mg daily for 4 more days, or clindamycin 300 mg four times a day, 3-7 days; azithromycin has higher resistance and clindamycin raises C. difficile risk even after one dose. About 10% self-report penicillin allergy; under 1% are truly allergic.

cites.quote: the panel suggests dentists prescribe oral cephalexin (500 milligrams, four times a day, 3–7d)

with a history of anaphylaxis, angioedema, or hives with penicillin, ampicillin, or amoxicillin, the panel suggests dentists prescribe oral azithromycin (loading dose of 500 milligrams on day 1, followed by 250 milligrams for an additional four days)
Although approximately 10% of the population self-reports a penicillin allergy, less than 1% of the entire population is truly allergic.

facts.claim: No response to first-line: add metronidazole 500 mg three times a day, 7 days, or switch to amoxicillin/clavulanate 500/125 mg three times a day, 7 days. Re-evaluate within 3 days; stop antibiotics 24 hours after symptoms completely resolve.

facts.claim: Definitive conservative dental treatment (DCDT) = pulpotomy, pulpectomy, root canal debridement, nonsurgical RCT or incision and drainage; extractions are outside this guideline's scope.

cites.quote: Definitive, conservative dental treatment refers to pulpotomy, pulpectomy, root canal debridement, non-surgical root canal treatment, or incision for drainage of abscess.

Metronidazole + alcohol: disulfiram-like reaction (cramps, nausea, vomiting, headache, flushing); no alcohol or propylene glycol during and for at least 3 days after. Don't give within 2 weeks of disulfiram (psychotic reactions). Can raise lithium levels.

facts.claim: First-line drugs for smoking cessation are nicotine replacement therapy, bupropion (an atypical antidepressant) and varenicline (a nicotine receptor partial agonist). Free telephone counseling is available through state quitlines at 1-800-QUIT-NOW.

facts.claim: CDC 2022 opioid guideline (recommendation 1): nonopioid therapies are at least as effective as opioids for many common acute pain conditions, and the guideline names dental pain and pain after minor surgery such as a simple dental extraction. Clinicians should make the most of nonopioid drugs (e.g., NSAIDs, acetaminophen) and nonpharmacologic therapies, consider an opioid for acute pain only if its expected benefits outweigh the risks, and discuss realistic benefits and known risks with the patient before prescribing one. The evidence review found opioids probably less effective than NSAIDs for surgical dental pain.
facts.conditions: Scope: outpatients aged 18 or older; the guideline excludes pain from sickle cell disease, cancer-related pain, palliative care and end-of-life care. ADA's own first-line recommendations are RX-1/RX-2.

cites.quote: Nonopioid therapies are at least as effective as opioids for many common types of acute pain.
only consider opioid therapy for acute pain if benefits are anticipated to outweigh risks to the patient
Before prescribing opioid therapy for acute pain, clinicians should discuss with patients the realistic benefits and known risks of opioid therapy

for outpatients aged ≥18 years, excluding pain management related to sickle cell disease, cancer-related pain treatment, palliative care, and end-of-life care

facts.claim: CDC 2022 (recommendations 3 and 4): when starting an opioid, prescribe an immediate-release opioid, not an extended-release/long-acting (ER/LA) one; ER/LA opioids should not be used to treat acute pain. For an opioid-naive patient, prescribe the lowest effective dosage, which is often about 5-10 morphine milligram equivalents (MME) per dose or 20-30 MME per day. For opioid-naive outpatients treated for a few days or less, dosage increases are usually unnecessary.
facts.conditions: The 5-10 MME and 20-30 MME/day figures are CDC's 'often equivalent' guide, not a fixed rule; the guideline says the lowest effective dose starts from product labeling. ADA's suggested opioid doses for dental pain are in RX-3.

cites.quote: clinicians should prescribe immediate-release opioids instead of extended-release and long-acting (ER/LA) opioids
Clinicians should not treat acute pain with ER/LA opioids

The lowest starting dose for opioid-naïve patients is often equivalent to a single dose of approximately 5–10 MME or a daily dosage of 20–30 MME/day.
For opioid-naïve outpatients with acute pain treated with an opioid for a few days or less, dosage increases are usually unnecessary

facts.claim: CDC 2022 (recommendation 6): when an opioid is needed for acute pain, prescribe no greater quantity than needed for the expected duration of pain severe enough to require an opioid; for many common causes of nontraumatic, nonsurgical pain, a few days or less is often enough. Avoid prescribing extra opioids just in case pain lasts longer than expected.
facts.conditions: CDC says durations should be individualized. Other sources give different numbers for the same decision: the ADA 2024 guideline says the duration rarely exceeds 3 days (RX-3), and ADA policy supports statutory limits of no more than 7 days (OPI-9). A stem must name its source.

cites.quote: When opioids are needed for acute pain, clinicians should prescribe no greater quantity than needed for the expected duration of pain severe enough to require opioids

Clinicians should generally avoid prescribing additional opioids to patients just in case pain continues longer than expected.

facts.claim: CDC 2022 (recommendation 8): before starting an opioid, evaluate the patient's risk for opioid-related harms (ask about drug and alcohol use) and build risk-reduction strategies into the plan, including offering naloxone. Offer naloxone when prescribing opioids, particularly to patients at increased risk of overdose: a history of overdose or of substance use disorder, sleep-disordered breathing, higher opioid dosages (e.g., 50 MME/day or more), or benzodiazepines taken with opioids.
facts.conditions: The CDC list also includes patients at risk of returning to a high dose to which they have lost tolerance (e.g., after tapering or release from prison). Giving naloxone in an overdose is EM-3.

cites.quote: Before starting and periodically during continuation of opioid therapy, clinicians should evaluate risk for opioid-related harms and discuss risk with patients.

Clinicians should ask patients about their drug and alcohol use

facts.claim: Check the state prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP) before prescribing an opioid: CDC 2022 (recommendation 9) says to review the patient's controlled-substance prescription history in the PDMP when prescribing initial opioid therapy for acute pain, ideally before every opioid prescription, to see whether the patient is receiving dosages or combinations that put them at high risk for overdose. The ADA (2016 statement) says dentists should register with and use their PDMP.
facts.conditions: CDC recommends PDMP review where PDMP access policies make it practicable (category B); state laws requiring a check vary and are not covered here.

cites.quote: clinicians should review the patient’s history of controlled substance prescriptions using state prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP) data to determine whether the patient is receiving opioid dosages or combinations that put the patient at high risk for overdose
Ideally, PDMP data should be reviewed before every opioid prescription for acute, subacute, or chronic pain.

facts.claim: Opioids plus benzodiazepines: CDC 2022 (recommendation 11) urges particular caution when prescribing an opioid together with a benzodiazepine, and weighing benefits and risks with other central nervous system depressants (e.g., muscle relaxants, nonbenzodiazepine sedative-hypnotics, gabapentin, pregabalin). Opioid labels carry a boxed warning that combining opioids with benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants, including alcohol, may cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death, so the combination is reserved for patients without adequate alternatives. CDC adds that buprenorphine or methadone for opioid use disorder should not be withheld from patients taking benzodiazepines.
facts.conditions: The sources state the general rule; they do not discuss dental oral sedation specifically. CDC notes some combinations can be appropriate (e.g., severe acute pain in a patient on long-term, stable low-dose benzodiazepine therapy).

facts.claim: Morphine milligram equivalents (MME, CDC 2022 table): multiply the daily dose of each opioid by its conversion factor: codeine 0.15, tramadol 0.2, hydrocodone 1.0, morphine 1.0, oxycodone 1.5, methadone 4.7, hydromorphone 5.0. Examples: hydrocodone 5 mg four times a day = 20 mg/day = 20 MME/day; oxycodone 10 mg twice a day = 20 mg/day = 30 MME/day. When opioids are continued for subacute or chronic pain, CDC says to use caution at any dosage, generally avoid dosage increases, and pause and carefully reassess benefits and risks before raising the total dosage to 50 MME/day or more. The factors are estimates, do not cover buprenorphine, are not used to work out doses when converting one opioid to another, and are not used for dosing in opioid use disorder treatment.
facts.conditions: Conversion factors differ between published tables, so a calculation item names CDC 2022. Overdose risk rises continuously with dosage and CDC says no single threshold eliminates risk: 50 MME/day is a point to pause and reassess for subacute or chronic opioid therapy, not a limit. Don't key an opioid-to-opioid dose conversion from MMEs (CDC says not to use them for that). Don't test the fentanyl, oxymorphone or tapentadol factors.

facts.claim: CDC 2022 (recommendation 12): clinicians should offer or arrange treatment with evidence-based medications for patients with opioid use disorder; detoxification alone, without medications for opioid use disorder, is not recommended because it raises the risks of resumed drug use, overdose and overdose death. For a patient with pain and active opioid use disorder who is not in treatment, consider buprenorphine or methadone treatment, which can also help manage the pain.
facts.conditions: For a general dentist, 'arrange' means referral; the guideline does not assign the prescribing role by specialty.

facts.claim: ADA statement on opioids for dental pain (2016): before prescribing an opioid, take a medical and dental history that covers current medications, possible drug interactions and any history of substance abuse; follow CDC and state licensing board recommendations; talk with patients about their responsibility for preventing misuse and abuse and for storing and disposing of opioids; consider NSAIDs first-line and multimodal strategies to spare opioids; and coordinate with the patient's other doctors, including pain specialists, when prescribing opioids for chronic orofacial pain.

cites.loc: ADA Statement on the Use of Opioids in the Treatment of Dental Pain (2016)
cites.quote: When considering prescribing opioids, dentists should conduct a medical and dental history to determine current medications, potential drug interactions and history of substance abuse.
Dentists should follow and continually review Centers for Disease Control and state licensing board recommendations for safe opioid prescribing.
Dentists should have a discussion with patients regarding their responsibilities for preventing misuse, abuse, storage and disposal of prescription opioids.
Dentists should consider nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics as the first-line therapy for acute pain management.
Dentists should recognize multimodal pain strategies for management for acute postoperative pain as a means for sparing the need for opioid analgesics.
Dentists should consider coordination with other treating doctors, including pain specialists when prescribing opioids for management of chronic orofacial pain.

facts.claim: Dental pain in a patient taking buprenorphine for opioid use disorder: the buprenorphine is not stopped (ADA: a patient with dental pain should not discontinue medication-assisted treatment), and nonopioid treatments are used for the pain (CDC 2022). For acute pain, CDC says clinicians can consider temporarily dosing buprenorphine more often (e.g., twice a day), because its pain-relieving effect is shorter than its effect on withdrawal. For severe acute pain (e.g., trauma or unplanned major surgery), additional as-needed buprenorphine doses can be considered, and in supervised settings a short-acting full agonist can be added without stopping buprenorphine. If buprenorphine is stopped instead, the patient must be monitored closely: high doses of a full agonist may be needed, risking oversedation and respiratory depression as buprenorphine's partial agonist effect wears off. Buprenorphine/naloxone (Suboxone) film itself is not appropriate as an analgesic: opioid-naive people have died after a 2 mg sublingual dose.
facts.conditions: Changing the buprenorphine dose or schedule belongs to its prescriber; a dentist coordinates with that prescriber. CDC's pain advice for patients on buprenorphine, methadone or naltrexone summarizes the ASAM 2020 focused update (CDC reference 96). Don't key an item on a dentist adding a full agonist on top of buprenorphine: CDC limits that option to severe acute pain (trauma, unplanned major surgery) in supervised settings.

facts.claim: Transmucosal buprenorphine (sublingual or buccal, e.g., Suboxone film) has an FDA label warning for dental problems: caries, some severe (tooth fracture, tooth loss), abscesses, erosion, lost fillings and even total tooth loss, reported even in patients with no prior dental problems. After the medicine has completely dissolved, the patient should take a large sip of water, swish it gently around the teeth and gums and swallow, and wait at least 1 hour before brushing. Dentists should do a baseline dental evaluation and caries risk assessment, set up a caries prevention plan (prescription fluoride toothpaste or trays can be considered) and encourage regular checkups. The ADA notes that the benefits of buprenorphine outweigh these risks and that professional oral care can help.
facts.conditions: The ADA handout's bullet list also says 'Rinse 30 min after use of strip/tab', which differs from the label and the handout's own patient section (rinse once the medicine has completely dissolved); key the label wording.

facts.claim: Acute pain in a patient on methadone maintenance for opioid use disorder: the existing methadone dose cannot be expected to relieve new acute pain (e.g., postoperative pain), and MAT is not stopped for dental pain (ADA). If opioids are needed, they are given in the doses otherwise indicated, and somewhat higher and/or more frequent doses are often needed because of methadone-induced tolerance (methadone label). CDC 2022: patients on methadone who need additional opioids for severe acute pain should be monitored carefully and, when feasible, treated in consultation with their opioid treatment program.
facts.conditions: Nonopioid treatment first still applies (CDC: use nonopioid pain treatments as appropriate, OPI-11). Whether to add opioids is the treating clinician's decision; for a general dentist the testable points are keep the methadone, expect tolerance, coordinate with the opioid treatment program.

facts.claim: Methadone boxed warnings that matter when a dentist prescribes: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes (also reported at doses used for maintenance treatment of opioid addiction), and cytochrome P450 interactions: inhibitors of CYP3A4, 2B6, 2C19, 2C9 or 2D6 can raise methadone levels and cause potentially fatal respiratory depression. The label's examples include macrolide antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin), azole antifungals (e.g., ketoconazole) and fluconazole; follow the patient closely and consider a methadone dose reduction with such changes.
facts.conditions: The methadone label names erythromycin and ketoconazole; clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A inhibitor per PK-1 but is not named in this label. Dose changes belong to the methadone prescriber or opioid treatment program.

facts.claim: Naltrexone (daily tablets, or a monthly extended-release injection, Vivitrol), used for opioid or alcohol dependence, is a competitive opioid antagonist: patients may not benefit from opioid analgesics (or opioid cough and antidiarrheal products), and the tablets are contraindicated in patients receiving opioid analgesics. The injection blocks opioids for about 28 days. Suggested pain management options are regional analgesia or nonopioid analgesics; the tablet label also lists conscious sedation with a benzodiazepine or general anesthesia, and CDC 2022 suggests short-term higher-potency nonopioids (e.g., NSAIDs) for severe acute pain. If opioid analgesia is unavoidable, more opioid than usual may be needed and the respiratory depression may be deeper and longer, so the patient must be closely monitored by trained personnel in a setting equipped for resuscitation.
facts.conditions: The labels frame these options for emergencies in patients on fully blocking doses; 'regional analgesia' is read as including dental local anesthesia, which the labels do not name. Opioid analgesia over a blockade is not office dentistry: don't key an item on a dentist doing it.

facts.claim: Overdose risks around naltrexone: the blockade is surmountable, so a patient who takes large opioid doses to overcome it risks life-threatening intoxication or fatal overdose; and after naltrexone is stopped (or the injection wears off), tolerance is lower, so doses once tolerated can be fatal. Naltrexone precipitates withdrawal in anyone physically dependent on opioids, so it is contraindicated in patients currently dependent on opioids, including those maintained on methadone or buprenorphine. The labels advise strongly considering a naloxone (overdose reversal agent) prescription.

cites.quote: Any attempt by a patient to overcome the antagonism by taking opioids is especially dangerous and may lead to life-threatening opioid intoxication or fatal overdose.

facts.claim: Signs of opioid overdose (CDC): unconsciousness or inability to wake the person; slow or shallow breathing or difficulty breathing, such as choking sounds or a gurgling or snoring noise; discolored skin (especially nails or lips); and small, constricted 'pinpoint' pupils that don't react to light. Opioid labels add somnolence progressing to stupor or coma, limp (flaccid) muscles and cold, clammy skin; with hypoxia the pupils may be markedly dilated instead. CDC: if unsure whether a person is high or overdosing, treat it as an overdose: give naloxone if available and call 911, try to keep the person awake and breathing, lay them on their side to prevent choking, and stay until help arrives.
facts.conditions: Naloxone dosing and repeat doses are in EM-3. The CDC page is written for bystanders; office airway management is OPI-18 and EM-4.

facts.claim: Treating an opioid overdose (opioid label): first secure a patent, protected airway and assisted or controlled ventilation if needed; give an opioid reversal agent such as naloxone (or nalmefene) for clinically significant respiratory or circulatory depression. The reversal is expected to wear off before codeine does, so monitor until spontaneous breathing is reliably reestablished and give more reversal agent if the response is suboptimal or brief. In a patient physically dependent on opioids, the usual reversal dose precipitates acute withdrawal, so if serious respiratory depression must be treated, start with care and titrate smaller doses.
facts.conditions: Taken from the acetaminophen/codeine label; other opioid labels carry the same overdose section. The 'reversal wears off first' point is stated for codeine in this label.

facts.claim: Codeine is converted by CYP2D6 to its active metabolite, morphine. CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolizers (e.g., gene duplications; estimated at 1-10% of Whites, 3-4% of Blacks and 1-2% of East Asians) convert it more rapidly and completely, so even labeled doses can produce higher-than-expected morphine levels and life-threatening or fatal respiratory depression; ultra-rapid metabolizers should not use codeine. After deaths in children (most after tonsillectomy and/or adenoidectomy, many ultra-rapid metabolizers), codeine is contraindicated in all children younger than 12 and for postoperative pain in children younger than 18 after tonsillectomy and/or adenoidectomy.
facts.conditions: RX-6 covers adolescents 12-18 with obesity, obstructive sleep apnea or severe lung disease, and breastfeeding. Prevalence figures are label estimates (over 10% in some other groups); don't key exact percentages.

facts.claim: Tramadol is also activated by CYP2D6, to O-desmethyltramadol (M1), which binds the mu-opioid receptor more potently than tramadol. Tramadol is contraindicated in all children younger than 12 and for postoperative pain in children younger than 18 after tonsillectomy and/or adenoidectomy.

facts.claim: Tramadol (a weak serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor as well as a mu-opioid agonist) can cause serotonin syndrome, particularly with serotonergic drugs such as SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclic antidepressants, triptans and MAO inhibitors, and seizures, even within the recommended dosage, with more risk above it and in patients taking SSRIs, tricyclics, other opioids, MAO inhibitors or neuroleptics, or with epilepsy or a history of seizures. It is contraindicated with an MAO inhibitor or within 14 days of one, and the dose must not exceed 400 mg a day.

facts.claim: Codeine interactions (boxed warning): CYP3A4 inhibitors such as macrolide antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin), azole antifungals (e.g., ketoconazole) and protease inhibitors (e.g., ritonavir), or stopping a CYP3A4 inducer (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin), raise codeine levels and, through CYP2D6, morphine levels, which can cause potentially fatal respiratory depression; if such an inhibitor is needed, consider a lower codeine dose and check often for respiratory depression and sedation. CYP2D6 inhibitors (e.g., amiodarone, quinidine) instead lower morphine levels, which can reduce pain relief or cause withdrawal. Tramadol's label also warns that using or stopping CYP3A4 inducers, CYP3A4 inhibitors or CYP2D6 inhibitors has complex effects that must be weighed for both tramadol and its active metabolite, M1.
facts.conditions: The label names erythromycin and ketoconazole; clarithromycin (a strong CYP3A inhibitor, PK-1) is covered only as a member of the macrolide class. Tramadol's warning exists but its specific effects are not detailed here.
